subject: Egress IP lease & firewall safeguards for private endpoint
messages:
From: Ben Turner <ben.turner@bluecorp.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, ops-security@acmehealth.com
Date: Thu, 05 Jun 2025 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Request - reserved egress IPs + firewall evidence for private endpoint

Hi Stephanie,

Thanks for taking this. We're in the final networking sign-off for the Acme Health private deployment. Security has an ask: they need a signed/leased set of static egress IPs we can allowlist in their perimeter firewall. Specific questions: 

- Can Redwood provide a short-term lease (30/90 days) on a small pool (2-4) of static IPv4 addresses that map to the private endpoint egress?
- How does Redwood handle NAT binding when we have multiple tenants behind the same connector? Will you guarantee stable source IPs per-tenant or per-connector?
- If you rotate the egress IPs, what's the notification window and how do you publish rotation events?
- We also need a minimal evidence pack for our compliance team: expected FQDNs/SNI to allow, ports, TLS requirements, and any recommended IDS/IPS bypass guidance.

I've attached our CSV with the fields we typically provide (acme_ip_request.csv). If you can send a single-page runbook we can hand to our firewall team that lists the IPs, TTL, and verification steps, that would be ideal.

Can we get an initial response today? We have a security gating call tomorrow.

Thanks,
Ben Turner
Network Operations
BlueCorp (on behalf of Acme Health)

Hi Ben —

Appreciate the clear list. Short answer: yes, we can support a leased set of egress IPs for private endpoints; below is our operational model and what we'll include in the evidence pack.

What Redwood will provide (high level):
- A reserved pool of IPv4 addresses bound to the customer private endpoint control plane for outbound connections. We can allocate 2–4 static IPs initially.
- Lease model: default 90-day renewable lease. We can accommodate 30-day for POCs but will document the exception and rotation policy.
- NAT binding: we bind by connector instance (per-tenant connector). That means stable source IPs while the connector is active. If customers use multi-tenant connectors we can offer dedicated connectors for strict separation.
- Rotation and notification: planned rotations are announced 14 days in advance via the HubSpot deal + our customer portal; emergency rotations may be shorter with_notify=72h plus immediate webhook for critical incidents.

Firewall/hardening guidance we'll include in the runbook:
- Allowlist: reserved IPv4 addresses (list will be provided as a single line CIDR or single-IP entries).
- Ports: primarily TCP 443 outbound to our controlplane/service FQDNs. Avoid allowing arbitrary ports — we will list any additional required ports per-integration.
- TLS: mTLS supported for control-plane channels; for egress to internet services we recommend TLS 1.2+ and validating SNI where possible.
- SNI/FQDN: We'll provide the canonical hostnames and expected SNI patterns (wildcard where applicable).
- IDS/IPS: Do not terminate TLS for Redwood traffic unless you can preserve SNI. If TLS interception is required, please work with us to confirm cert pinning expectations.

Evidence we will ship: IP list (CSV), allowlist template (redwood-allowlist-template.xlsx), a one-page runbook with TTL/rotation cadence, and a short test script to verify source IP (curl + --resolve sample).

Next steps: I'll have a technical note from David with NAT specifics and a draft runbook attached. Marissa will coordinate the SLA exception if you want a shorter 30-day lease.

---
Stephanie Nguyen

On Thu, Jun 5, 2025 at 9:12 AM Ben Turner <ben.turner@bluecorp.com> wrote:
> We're in the final networking sign-off for the Acme Health private deployment...

Ben — quick technical addendum to make the runbook actionable for your ops team: 

1) Allocation model and NAT binding
- We allocate static /32s (individual IPv4) per-customer connector; for HA you can expect 2 IPs (active/standby).
- Source NAT (SNAT) is applied at the gateway; outbound sockets from the connector will preserve a stable source IP while the connector process remains bound to that SNAT entry.
- If you request dedicated connectors per-tenant we guarantee per-tenant stable SNAT entries. Multi-tenant connectors may exhibit ephemeral port reuse but will keep the same source IP.

2) Lease TTL and rotation
- Default lease: 90 days. For short leases (30 days) we'll tag as POC and add an SLA exception (see Marissa).
- Rotation process: new IPs are allocated and populated in the egress mapping table; connections are drained over a 48-hour window. We publish planned rotations on the HubSpot deal + portal and queue webhooks for programmatic consumption.

3) Firewall specifics to include verbatim in the runbook
- Allowed source: the static IPv4 addresses we provide. If you consume them as CIDR, we will specify exact mask (usually /32).
- Allowed destination: our controlplane and model-serving FQDNs (list included). Use port 443 (TLS).
- SNI policy: allow SNI for hostnames in the list; do not perform deep TLS interception unless you can re-sign and preserve SNI.
- Keep-alive/timeouts: we recommend idle TCP timeout >= 300s for long-lived streaming sessions.

4) Observability & verification
- We'll provide a small verification script (curl + external IP echo) and a set of sample logs.
- Enable flow logs and provide a window where Redwood can validate flows during onboarding.

5) Edge considerations
- If Acme enforces outbound proxying, we recommend allowing our connector to use a direct NAT path. Proxied egress can break long-lived streams and increase latency.

I'll drop these into the runbook draft as explicit bullets. If your firewall team needs a PSA describing why TLS interception breaks streaming, I can add a section with packet-level examples.

-David
David Kim
Platform Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference
